content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate chip cookie is a fragrant biscuit made from a home recipe or purchased at a bakery. The dough typically consists of flour, butter, sugar, eggs, and chocolate chips, giving it a crisp edge and a soft, slightly chewy center.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate chip cookie recipes appeared in the United States in the 1930s.
A homemade version allows you to control sugar levels and use whole‑grain flour for a healthier option.
Chocolate chips are often made from dark chocolate, increasing antioxidant content.
Cookies are commonly served with tea or coffee, as the sweetness balances the bitterness of the drinks.
In some countries, chocolate chip cookies are a traditional treat at children’s parties.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates and a modest amount of fat provides a quick boost of energy.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate chips are rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Small amounts of magnesium and tryptophan in the cookie may contribute to improved mood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and whole‑grain flour supply B1, B2, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from dairy
items.content: If the recipe uses milk or butter, the cookie becomes a source of calcium beneficial for bones.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption can contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional cookies contain wheat flour, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Dairy protein allergy
items.content: Butter and milk may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or casein allergy.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some commercial varieties may contain partially hydrogenated oils, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Risk of over‑eating
items.content: The crunchy texture and sweet taste encourage rapid consumption of large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chocolate chip cookies can be enjoyed as a snack on their own, added to ice cream or yogurt, or used as layers in dessert cakes. When baked at home, you can control portion size by making smaller cookies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cookies in an airtight container at room temperature in a dry place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent softening from moisture. Discard any cookies that become soggy, moldy, or develop an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Eggnog is a traditional holiday drink made from milk, cream, eggs, sugar, and spices, often spiked with alcohol such as rum, brandy, or whiskey. It has a thick, creamy texture and a distinctive aroma of cinnamon, nutmeg, and vanilla.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggnog originated in medieval England, where it was made from egg yolks, milk, and spices.
The drink became popular in colonial America and has since become a symbol of Christmas celebrations.
Nutmeg is a classic ingredient that gives eggnog its characteristic warm, slightly spicy flavor.
There are many variations: non‑alcoholic, vegan (using plant‑based milk), and versions with different spirits.
In some parts of the United States, frozen eggnog (“frosted eggnog”) is served as a dessert.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs, the main ingredient, provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggnog contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Milk and cream supply calcium and vitamin D, important for bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Cinnamon and nutmeg contain polyphenols with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Sugar and fats provide a quick source of energy, useful in cold weather.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Raw eggs may harbor salmonella; use pasteurized eggs or heat‑treat the mixture.

items.title: High in sugar and fat
items.content: Eggnog is calorie‑dense; people watching weight or blood sugar should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Alcoholic versions can be unsafe for children, pregnant individuals, and those with liver issues.

items.title: Milk allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: Those with dairy sensitivities should choose dairy‑free alternatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eggnog is served chilled in glasses or mugs, often topped with a sprinkle of ground cinnamon or nutmeg. It can be homemade using pasteurized eggs or bought ready‑to‑drink. Non‑alcoholic versions are suitable for children and anyone avoiding spirits.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared eggnog in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days in a sealed container. For longer storage, it can be frozen, though the texture may change. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or signs of spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Pretzels are crunchy snack twists made from wheat flour, water, salt and yeast. This version is coated with a smooth yogurt layer that adds a mild tang and creamy flavor while preserving the characteristic crisp texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pretzels have a medieval European origin, with early forms dating back to the Middle Ages.
The traditional knot shape symbolizes crossed arms, a sign of good luck.
Yogurt coating is often used to reduce sugar compared with chocolate or caramel variants.
In the United States, yogurt‑coated pretzel sales grew over 30 % in the 2020s due to rising demand for “better‑for‑you” snacks.
While classic pretzels are a popular beer accompaniment, the yogurt version pairs well with fruit dips.

items.title: Rich in complex carbs
items.content: The wheat base provides sustained energy release, helping to keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Yogurt coating typically contains less added sugar than chocolate‑coated alternatives.

items.title: Source of probiotics
items.content: Some yogurt coatings include live cultures that support gut health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins and iron
items.content: Wheat flour and yeast contribute B‑vitamins and a modest amount of iron.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The slight acidity of yogurt can help improve nutrient absorption.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Pretzels contain wheat, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: The yogurt coating may contain lactose, which should be considered by those with intolerance.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Despite lower sugar, the snack remains energy‑dense; portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Like many baked snacks, pretzels can be relatively high in salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy pretzels straight from the bag, dip them in fruit or berry sauces, add them to salads for crunch, or incorporate them into snack mixes with cheese and nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage (over 2–3 weeks) refrigerate to maintain crispness and prevent the yogurt coating from softening.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetarian pho is a fragrant Vietnamese soup made with a clear vegetable or mushroom broth, rice noodles, fresh herbs, and spices. It retains the signature aroma of traditional pho while being completely plant‑based, making it suitable for vegetarians and vegans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Classic pho is cooked in a beef broth, but the vegetarian version uses mushroom or vegetable stock.
Rice noodles are thin and quickly absorb the broth’s flavor.
Herbs such as basil, cilantro, and mint are added just before serving to keep them fresh.
Pho is commonly served with lime, chili, and soy sauce, allowing each diner to customize the taste.
Vietnamese cuisine is considered one of the healthiest thanks to its abundant fresh herbs and vegetables.

items.title: Rich in vegetables
items.content: The soup provides carrots, onions, celery, and mushrooms, delivering vitamins A, C, and B‑complex.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Without meat or fatty stocks, vegetarian pho is relatively low‑calorie, supporting weight management.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Spices like ginger, cinnamon, and cloves aid digestion and have anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Tofu and mushrooms add a complete set of essential amino acids.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The broth helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Tofu and soy sauce can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared soy sauce is often salty; choose low‑sodium versions when possible.

items.title: Gluten in noodles
items.content: Some rice noodles are processed with gluten; opt for certified gluten‑free varieties.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the broth, add noodles, tofu, mushrooms, and vegetables. Serve with lime wedges, fresh mint, cilantro, sliced chili, and soy sauce to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the broth refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Store noodles and fresh herbs separately; noodles can be frozen for up to 1 month.

content.title: About
content.content: Spanish rice is a dish made from long‑grain rice cooked with tomatoes, bell pepper, onion, garlic and spices such as paprika and saffron. It often includes peas, carrots and meat (chicken, sausage or seafood). The dish has a vivid red color and a rich aroma typical of Mediterranean cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally the dish is cooked in a single pot, allowing the rice to absorb all the flavors.
The name “Spanish” comes from the use of spices originally imported from Spain, like saffron.
In Mexico a similar dish is called “arroz a la mexicana”, while in the US it is known as “Spanish rice” or “Mexican rice”.
It is commonly served as a side to tacos, fajitas and other Mexican‑style meals.
Vegetarian versions omit meat and add beans or tofu instead.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides sustained energy and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3 and B6 support carbohydrate metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and paprika are high in lycopene and vitamin C, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables and rice promotes healthy bowel movements.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The dish is typically prepared with minimal oil, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Spanish rice is often seasoned with salt; people monitoring sodium intake should adjust accordingly.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to paprika, saffron or garlic.

items.title: Gluten in additives
items.content: If broth or sauces contain gluten, choose gluten‑free alternatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Spanish rice hot as a side to meat, fish or vegetarian dishes. Garnish with fresh herbs (parsley, cilantro) and a squeeze of lime. Leftover rice reheats well in the microwave or skillet with a splash of water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked Spanish rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.
